Chapter 5: The Relationship Between Owners and Managers
Let’s dive into something that often flies under the radar, but it’s really at the core of every strong business—the relationship between owners and managers.
Picture this: a small business where the owner’s right there on the floor, rolling up their sleeves, making decisions with the team, and sharing in both the risks and the rewards. There’s a real sense of partnership, right? Everyone’s moving toward the same goal, and you can feel that collective energy.
Now, let’s shift gears and think bigger. In large companies, things aren’t always so simple. Owners, usually shareholders, are often miles away from the day-to-day action. There are layers of managers, and sometimes it’s easy for their interests to go in different directions. Managers might start focusing more on their own goals instead of what’s best for the owners.
So, what do the best companies do to fix this? They find ways to bring managers and owners back onto the same page. Sometimes that means tying bonuses or pay to how well the company does in the long run, or letting managers have an actual stake—a piece of the company’s success.
But here’s something to pay attention to: alignment isn’t just about money. It’s built on trust, good communication, and shared values. When managers start thinking like owners—caring about the health of the business years down the road, not just the next quarterly report—everybody wins.
Think about a company that lets employees buy shares at a discount. Suddenly, people see themselves as part-owners. Over time, this sense of ownership completely changes how they work. They’re more careful with resources, speak up when they spot a problem, and feel a deeper commitment to the company’s success.
Of course, it’s not always smooth sailing. Not every manager puts the owners first. Some might chase personal gain, take unnecessary risks, or even sweep bad news under the rug. That’s why it’s so important for owners to stay involved, ask tough questions, and hold managers accountable.
Here’s the bottom line: transparency is essential. Owners need clear, honest updates about how things are going, and managers need to be upfront about their choices and plans. If communication breaks down, trust falls apart, and the whole company feels it.
Over time, companies that really nurture strong relationships between owners and managers tend to pull ahead. They make smarter decisions, adapt quicker when things change, and create more value for everyone involved.
